items.title: The Fairphone 6 Plus is modular, repairable, and $100 off right now
items.raw:
The Fairphone 6 Plus comes with 12 replaceable parts. | Photo: Dominic Preston / The Verge	

Unlike most smartphones, the Fairphone 6 Plus is designed for home repair, with easily replaceable parts that could help extend its lifespan well into the future. That makes its midrange price point easier to justify, especially now that it’s dropped to a new low of $552.49 (about $98 off) at Amazon as part of the retailer’s ongoing Black Friday sale.
Fairphone 6 Plus

Where to Buy:

 $649.99 $552.49 at Amazon (black)
 $649.99 $552.49 at Amazon (green)
 $649.99 $552.49 at Amazon (blue)

The 6.3-inch Fairphone 6 Plus features 12 user-replaceable parts, including the battery, screen, USB-C port, and cameras, all of which you can swap out with the included screwdriver. Replacement parts are relatively affordable, too; a new battery costs $39.99, which helps offset its middling battery life and lack of wireless charging. It also comes with a five-year warranty and up to six Android OS upgrades, making it a good option if you want a phone you can keep using for years.
Although repairability is its marquee feature, the 6 Plus is also a solid midrange Android device. Fairphone prioritizes ethically sourced materials, making it a strong choice for environmentally conscious buyers who don’t want to sacrifice performance. Its Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 processor handles everyday tasks well, and its cameras take decent photos, though they’re not quite on par with those of pricier phones.
What’s more, it offers a clean, bloatware-free Android experience and modular back panels, which you can swap for optional accessories like a card holder or crossbody strap. Our own Allison Johnson particularly liked the phone’s dedicated switch for turning on customizable focus modes called Moments, which can simplify your homescreen and limit access to distracting apps — something we could all use a little less of.
Read our full Fairphone 6 Plus review.

items.title: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
items.raw:
Kishanth Peramalya was denied entry due to sexual assault convictions and sent to Africa where he had no connections
The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.
Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.

Concerns over Beijing’s use of ‘red notices’ as Hong Kong prepares to host police organisation’s general assembly
China is misusing Interpol to target and silence dissidents, a leading British lawyer has claimed, as Hong Kong prepares to host the police organisation’s general assembly for the first time.
Ben Keith, a specialist in “red notices” - the Interpol system under which national authorities are requested to locate and detain suspects - said he was working on five cases involving China making questionable requests through Interpol.

items.title: Pro-Palestine activist sought by US in extradition case: ‘I still have a right to my beliefs’
items.raw:
James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, at center of legal fight, says he ‘should not be unjustly accused’ because of leftwing views
James “Fergie” Chambers, the wealthy leftwing activist and donor controversially sought in extradition by the US, has told the Guardian that he is “not asking anyone to endorse my ideas or not think I’m a jerk – but I still have a right to my beliefs and should not be unjustly accused because of them”.
Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.

items.title: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
items.raw:
Exclusive: Records list 349 deaths in three years in Mali and also shed light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa
When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted.
“Everything was happening at once. Explosions were going off all around us, people were shouting,” recalled a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps who was stationed in Mali at the time and spoke on condition of anonymity. “Nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.”
